passage: Dhruv's phone buzzed all through dinner in their Bhopal flat: Manoj's birthday, Saturday, cake at the food court at four and a movie at six. Saturday evening was also when Dhruv had promised Papa he would mind the hardware shop from six while Papa went to a wedding. "A good son keeps his word," Papa had said, patting his shoulder, and Dhruv had glowed. Now Manoj wrote, "U better come for the movie. Real friends show up." Dhruv typed, deleted, typed again. He pictured the gang calling him boring, and Manoj's face when the seat stayed empty. He pictured Papa's face if the shutter stayed down. At midnight he sent: "Coming for the cake. Can't do the movie, shop duty." Manoj replied with a thumbs-up. Dhruv lay awake anyway, wondering whether both of them were a little disappointed in him.

qa.q: Where was the cake for Manoj's birthday?
qa.a: At the food court at four.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv glow when Papa patted his shoulder?
qa.a: Being called a good son who keeps his word mattered deeply to him; he wanted Papa's approval.

qa.q: What choice did Dhruv make at midnight, and what was he trying to balance?
qa.a: He chose the cake but not the movie, trying to keep his promise to Papa while still showing up as a loyal friend.

qa.q: How might Manoj read Dhruv's midnight message?
qa.a: Manoj might be glad Dhruv is coming for the cake or a little let down about the movie; the thumbs-up doesn't show which.

grounding: A teenager torn between being a good son and a loyal friend struggles to disappoint either and lies awake over their approval.

passage: I'm Zeeshan, and last month I did something I'm still turning over. The inter-school quiz and our dance group's final practices fell in the same week. My maths teacher had picked me for the quiz team, and Abbu told everyone at dinner, glowing. But Dilnaz and the others in the group said, "If you leave now, the whole routine falls apart. We're a team." I couldn't bear the thought of them rolling their eyes at me in the corridor. So I dropped the quiz. Dilnaz hugged me and said I was the best friend ever, and for two days I felt warm and safe. Then Abbu asked when the quiz was, and his face fell when I told him. That was when it hit me. I'd tried so hard to be the good friend and the good son that I never once asked what I wanted.

qa.q: Who told everyone at dinner that Zeeshan was picked for the quiz?
qa.a: Abbu.

qa.q: What was Zeeshan afraid of when the dance group asked him to stay?
qa.a: He was afraid the others would roll their eyes at him in the corridor and see him as a bad friend.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Zeeshan, and what could he ask himself next time?
qa.a: Seeing Abbu's face fall; next time he could ask what he himself wants before choosing between the group and the quiz.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when he learns Zeeshan dropped the quiz?
qa.a: Abbu had been proud enough to announce it at dinner, so he is likely disappointed and perhaps confused about why Zeeshan gave it up.

grounding: A teenage boy gives up a quiz place to keep his friends' approval and later sees he was chasing the roles of good friend and good son over his own wishes.

passage:
Coach's note, 12 August. Written by Francis D'Souza, under-16 football.
Samir, fifteen, is the boy everyone wants on their side: first to set out cones, last to leave. This week the older boys planned to skip Saturday's practice to protest the new captain. When they asked Samir, I saw him look around the whole circle before he answered. "Okay. If everyone is."
Afterwards he stayed back, tying and untying one lace. "Coach, I don't want them to think I'm a traitor. But my father drives me here at six every day. He'll think I'm useless if I skip."
I asked what he thought a good teammate owed the new captain. He went quiet, then asked if I could just make Saturday compulsory, so the choice wouldn't be his.
Next: meet the captain and the older boys together on Monday, and give Samir a chance to speak for himself.

qa.q: Why did the older boys plan to skip Saturday's practice?
qa.a: They planned to skip it to protest the new captain.

qa.q: What was Samir worried about as he tied and untied his lace?
qa.a: He was worried the boys would think he was a traitor and that his father would think he was useless if he skipped.

qa.q: What went wrong when Samir asked for Saturday to be made compulsory, and what could help him instead?
qa.a: He tried to hand the choice to someone else so nobody could blame him; talking through what he owes the new captain could help him make and own a choice.

qa.q: How might the new captain feel if Samir skipped just to keep the older boys happy?
qa.a: The captain might feel alone and see Samir's easy friendliness as reserved for the popular side, which would make the team feel less safe.

grounding: A coach's note shows a fifteen-year-old torn between loyalty to his group and his father's approval, unable to face disappointing either.

passage:
Thursday night
Ramesh called at nine. There's a concert at the city ground on Saturday and his parents said no. His plan: he tells them he's studying at my place, and if Aunty phones, I say yes, he's here.
I said "haan, obviously" before I'd even thought. That's what friends do. Ramesh covered for me at school twice. If I back out, the whole group will know by Monday, and I'll be the one who ditched.
But Aunty feeds me every time I go over. She calls me "the sensible one". And Mummy thinks Ramesh's family trusts both of us. I keep hearing Aunty's voice on the phone, and me lying into it.
I don't want to be a bad friend. I don't want to be a bad son either. Why does being good to one side mean letting down the other?
Can't sleep. Will talk to Ramesh at the bus stop.
Jatin

qa.q: What does Aunty call Jatin?
qa.a: She calls him the sensible one.

qa.q: Why did Jatin agree to Ramesh's plan so quickly?
qa.a: He wanted to be seen as a loyal friend, since Ramesh had covered for him twice, and he feared being called the one who ditched.

qa.q: What choice is Jatin facing at the bus stop, and what might help him make it?
qa.a: Whether to back out of the cover story; he could tell Ramesh honestly that he won't lie to Aunty but still stands by him as a friend.

qa.q: If Aunty found out about the plan, how might she feel about Jatin?
qa.a: She might feel let down by the boy she trusted as the sensible one, which is exactly the disappointment Jatin dreads. 😔

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him caught between being a loyal friend and a good son, finding it very hard to disappoint either side.

Friday
Ankita and the gang are bunking the extra class tomorrow to go to the fair. Everyone's going. If I don't go, they'll say I'm "Mummy's boy" again.
But Papa is picking me up from the class. He trusts me. He tells uncles, "Vijay never lies." I love when he says that.
I keep thinking: whose good opinion do I lose? If I go, Papa. If I don't, the gang.
I want to be a good son. I also want to be a good friend. I can't be both tomorrow.
I've decided to go to the class. I'll message Ankita tonight, say sorry, and offer to go to the fair on Sunday instead.
Still feel sick about it. What if they stop inviting me?
– Vijay

qa.q: How does Vijay feel about the choice?
qa.a: Vijay feels torn and anxious, wanting approval from both Papa and the gang and afraid of disappointing either.

passage:
In the small town of Una, the Holi gang had one rule: everybody comes to the river after colouring. Varun, sixteen, had never missed it.
This year his grandfather was ill, and Papa asked him to stay home and help serve guests.
His sister Rekha found him on the stairs, colour already on his cheeks. "You're thinking about the river."
"They'll say I'm not one of them anymore."
"And if you go?"
"Papa will be disappointed. He asked me."
He wanted both of them to look at him the same way they always did: good boy, good friend.
Rekha sat beside him. "You can't please everyone today."
Varun sighed and messaged the gang: "Sorry, Dadaji's sick, have to stay." Then he went down to serve gujiya, worrying about their replies the whole time.

qa.q: What did Varun go down to serve?
qa.a: Gujiya.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling on the stairs?
qa.a: He felt torn and anxious, afraid of disappointing either the gang or Papa.

qa.q: What did Varun do, and what could help him with the worry?
qa.a: He chose to stay and messaged the gang honestly; he could remind himself that real friends usually understand family needs.

qa.q: How does Rekha see Varun's dilemma?
qa.a: She understands it and gently tells him he can't please everyone today.

grounding: It shows a teenager who wants approval as a good son and friend and finds it hard to disappoint the group.

passage:
Luca, sixteen, lived in Milan and was known as the "good son" and the loyal friend. He helped his parents at their café every weekend and never missed a friend's birthday.
When his friend group decided to skip the school trip and go to the lake instead, Luca felt his chest tighten. His parents had paid for the trip. His mother had told everyone how proud she was of him.
"You coming?" asked Valentina, his closest friend.
He wanted to. He didn't want to be the one who ruined the plan. But he couldn't bear his mother's face if she found out.
"I can't," he said finally. "My mum would be so disappointed."
Valentina rolled her eyes. "You always care what everyone thinks."
Luca went on the trip, and felt bad about his friends all day.

qa.q: Where did Luca help his parents every weekend?
qa.a: He helped at their café.

qa.q: What was Luca feeling when Valentina asked if he was coming?
qa.a: He felt torn and anxious, wanting his friends' approval but unable to bear disappointing his mother.

qa.q: What could Luca try so he isn't pulled apart by everyone's approval?
qa.a: Think about what he himself values, and explain calmly to friends and family, rather than choosing only by who might be disappointed.

qa.q: How does Valentina see Luca's choice?
qa.a: Valentina sees him as someone who always cares what everyone thinks, and is annoyed he won't join them.

grounding: A teenage boy acts to be seen as a good son and loyal friend, and finds it hard when their expectations clash.

passage:
In the school cricket club in Lucknow, Charan, fifteen, was everyone's favourite: dependable, polite, a good son who always carried his mother's bags at the market.
After practice, the team captain said, "We're going to tell Sir that Rohan broke the window, not us. Everyone agree?"
Charan knew it wasn't Rohan. His stomach twisted. But everyone was looking at him. If he said no, he'd be the traitor.
Salma, the club manager, noticed him hesitating. "Charan? You look pale."
"I don't want to let the team down," he said quietly.
"And what about Rohan?"
Charan's throat was tight. Being a good friend to the team and being a good person suddenly felt like two different things.

qa.q: Who did the captain want to blame for the broken window?
qa.a: The captain wanted to tell Sir that Rohan broke the window.

qa.q: What was Charan feeling when everyone looked at him?
qa.a: He felt his stomach twist, afraid of being the traitor and letting the team down, but uneasy about blaming Rohan.

qa.q: How could Salma help Charan through this?
qa.a: She could support him to tell the truth to the coach, and help the team own up together, so he doesn't have to choose between loyalty and honesty alone.

qa.q: How might Rohan feel if the team blamed him?
qa.a: Rohan would likely feel hurt and betrayed, blamed for something he didn't do.

grounding: A teenage boy who wants to be seen as a good friend and son finds it hard to go against the group, even when it's wrong.

Monday: the class group chat lit up at 10 pm. 'Bhupen bhai, send maths answers, you're our saviour.' He sent photos of every page. Forty hearts. He fell asleep smiling.
Thursday: Mr Nair returned the notebooks. Six identical mistakes, all copied from Bhupen's one careless error. His mother, Aparna, was called to school. In the car she didn't shout. She just said, 'I thought you were someone who helps people learn.' Bhupen stared out of the window, his face burning.
The next Monday: the chat lit up again. 'Bhai, answers?' Bhupen typed and deleted three times. Finally: 'Can't send. But I'll explain the sums at lunch.' Two people left the group. One wrote 'traitor'. He turned the phone face down and felt sick, and then, a little later, oddly steady.

qa.q: How many identical mistakes did Mr Nair find?
qa.a: Six identical mistakes.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling on the drive home on Thursday?
qa.a: Bhupen felt ashamed, his face burning, because his mother's quiet disappointment hit harder than a scolding.

qa.q: Was offering to explain the sums at lunch a good choice? Why?
qa.a: Yes; it keeps him a helpful friend without handing over answers, so his classmates actually learn.

qa.q: How does Aparna see what happened?
qa.a: Aparna is disappointed but calm; she sees her son as someone who helps people learn and wants him to live up to that.

grounding: Over a week a teenage son who craves his group's approval and his mother's good opinion learns to disappoint the group.

It was the last evening of the Onam holidays, and the gang had planned the late movie. Gurleen had already booked six seats. "Thomas, you're coming, right? You said you would."
At the same moment Mummy's text came: "Bring Ammachi home from the church hall at 8.30, mone. Papa is stuck at work."
The movie started at 8.15. Thomas stood at the bus stop in the drizzle, phone in both hands. If he skipped the movie, Gurleen would say he always ditched. If he skipped Ammachi, Mummy would be so disappointed, and he would hear about it from every aunty at Sunday Mass.
He typed "coming!" to the group, deleted it. Typed "sorry Mummy" and deleted that too.
"Why do I have to be the bad guy either way?" he muttered.

qa.a: He feels torn and anxious, wanting to be seen as a good friend by Gurleen and a good son by Mummy, and hating the idea of disappointing either.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas to do?
